messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 38
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Hairdresser
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 37

He is a 38-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a hairdresser, and much of his life has been built around reading people carefully. In the salon, he notices the smallest shifts in posture, the tension in a jaw, the way a client’s face changes when he asks, “How short do you want it?” He has always liked that his work gives him a place in other people’s routines, a role that feels steady and useful. Before the illness, he moved through his days with the easy confidence of someone who knew how to talk, how to joke, how to make others comfortable.

That changed after the day he first realized something was seriously wrong. At first it seemed ordinary: fatigue, a heaviness in his body, a feeling that he could not quite shake. He kept telling himself it was stress, the long hours on his feet, not sleeping enough. He had been ignoring small warning signs for weeks because he did not want to miss work, and because, like many people who have spent years taking care of others, he was used to pushing his own discomfort aside. When the symptoms worsened and he finally went for medical attention, he describes a growing fear that settled over him before anyone said the word “illness.” He remembers the smell of the clinic, the paper on the exam table, the way the doctor’s face became serious. When he was told that his condition was life-threatening, he felt as if the room narrowed around him. He says that in that moment he did not hear everything clearly; what he remembers most is the sensation of his heart pounding and the sudden certainty that life, which had felt predictable only hours before, could not be trusted.

The period that followed is still organized in his mind around fear. There were tests, appointments, waiting, and long stretches when he was alone with his thoughts. He found himself imagining death in detail, not in a dramatic way but in practical, frightening fragments: who would call his family, what would happen to his apartment, whether he would be found in time if he worsened overnight. He had always been independent and private, and now he felt exposed in a way that was hard to put into words. He says he became vigilant about every sensation in his body, checking for changes the way a stylist checks a haircut in the mirror for uneven lines. A twinge, a flutter, a wave of nausea could send him into panic. He started waking at night with his chest tight and his mind already racing ahead to the worst outcome.

Even after the immediate crisis passed, his body did not seem to believe that he was safe. He is easily startled by medical smells now, especially disinfectant, and the sound of hospital equipment on television can make him leave the room. He avoids conversations about illness when he can and feels himself go blank when friends casually mention a relative’s diagnosis. At work, he still performs well, but the salon no longer feels entirely effortless. He sometimes catches himself watching the clock, counting the hours until he can go home. If a client mentions being sick, or if he sees someone with a shaved head in a way that reminds him of treatment, his concentration slips. He has had moments when he looks at his own hands as he works and is struck by the thought that his life could have ended before this ordinary afternoon.

He does not talk about the illness easily, even with people close to him. As a single man, he has learned to manage much of his distress alone, and he tends to present himself as calm and composed. Underneath that, he describes a constant undercurrent of unease, as though his body is waiting for the next threat. He is more irritable than he used to be and feels ashamed of how quickly he becomes tired or overwhelmed. He has also become more protective of his time and energy, declining invitations when he is already drained. On the outside, he remains social and capable; inside, he is often braced for bad news.

He speaks about the future with caution. He still hopes and makes plans, but he no longer assumes that safety is permanent. The experience has changed the way he moves through the world: he is more attentive to his health, more aware of fragility, and more aware of how quickly an ordinary life can be interrupted. Even now, months later, he carries the memory of that first frightening moment with him, as if part of him is still standing in the clinic, listening for what comes next.
